blocks.text: I first met Brandei Estes back in 2024 at Chaussee 36, where she curated the wonderful exhibition SMORGASBORD by Maisie Cousins. Since then, we’ve crossed paths at Paris Photo and on several other occasions, so I wanted to find out more about Brandei’s career and personal story. Join me for our “Beyond the Print” conversation, and enjoy the read!

Nadine Dinter: Brandei, you are working as Acting Senior Curator of Photographs at the National Portrait Gallery, London as well as an Independent Photographs Curator and Advisor. How does a regular work day look like for you?

Brandei Estes: No two days are ever quite the same, which is one of the things I enjoy most about my work. I might spend the morning moderating a conversation with an artist represented in the Gallery’s collection, as I did this morning, followed by meetings with colleagues across different departments. I try to work from home one day a week, allowing myself some uninterrupted time for research, writing, correspondence and reflection.

Some of my favourite moments, however, are spent in curatorial meetings, discussing the ethics and responsibilities of acquiring particular works for the national collection. We are constantly asking ourselves how we want to preserve our present for future generations, what that present looks like, and whose stories we are telling. These are fascinating conversations, and ones that remind me of the significance of what we do.

I also love the physical process of curating exhibitions, particularly the installation period when months, sometimes years, of research and planning finally come together. It reminds me of preparing an elaborate dinner party: setting the table, making the final adjustments and anticipating the moment when everyone arrives to enjoy what you have created. Ultimately, I’m a team player, and I particularly value the collaborative nature of museum work, the constant exchange of ideas and the collective responsibility for shaping something meaningful.
Prior to the mentioned job, you worked as the Head of Photographs at Sotheby’s (EMEA), London. Could you share one memorable highlight from your time there?

BE: There are so many memories, but two moments particularly stand out. The first was taking my inaugural auction as an auctioneer, which was nerve-racking and exhilarating in equal measure. There is nothing quite like the theatre of an auction room, the anticipation, the energy and the responsibility of orchestrating it all in real time.

The second was a much quieter, solitary experience during lockdown. I had gone into Sotheby’s warehouse to catalogue works for an upcoming sale and found myself sitting alone, holding a vintage photograph by Ana Mendieta that she had printed herself. I remember being profoundly moved by the intimacy of that encounter. Here was an object that had passed through the artist’s own hands, carrying both the physical traces of her practice and the conceptual weight of her work. It felt enormous and humbling, and I remember thinking how privileged I was to be entrusted with researching, cataloguing and ultimately selling something of such artistic significance.
Why Photography?

BE: I came to photography through work and fell in love with it almost immediately. My degree in History of Art and Italian focused primarily on the Italian High Renaissance, but being a teenager and then a university student in London during the late 1990s was an extraordinary time to encounter contemporary art. I still vividly remember seeing Sensation at the Royal Academy in 1997 and having my mind completely blown.

What particularly captivated me was the way contemporary artists were using photography, not simply as a means of recording the world, but as a medium through which to question, construct and challenge it. The possibilities seemed limitless, both conceptually and materially. This curiosity led me to explore the history of photography more deeply, discovering its extraordinary canon and the many ways in which artists have continually reinvented the medium.

I subsequently spent a decade working in photography galleries before joining Sotheby’s. Those formative years gave me an invaluable understanding of the relationship between artists, collectors and the market, but perhaps more importantly, they taught me how to look at photographs and appreciate the extraordinary complexity of what can initially appear to be such a familiar medium.
When did you enter the world of photography? And what is your connection?

BE: My first job after university was at David Gill Galleries, an extraordinarily forward-thinking space dedicated to contemporary art and design. David and his partner Francis had a remarkable personal art collection, which included several important photographic works. It was here, in the early 2000s, that I first began to understand photography as a serious collecting discipline, and to appreciate how naturally it could sit alongside painting, sculpture and design.

About two years later, I moved to Michael Hoppen Gallery, and the rest, as they say, is history! I was one of several sales associates working for Michael, and we were quite a large team at the time. It was an exciting, demanding and often challenging environment, but I learnt an enormous amount. We were working closely with artists, collectors and institutions, and I was fortunate to be surrounded by people with a deep knowledge and love of photography. Those years really established the foundations of my career and my enduring connection to the medium.
You have worked in the UK but work on an international scale including world-wide travel? How’s the photography market compared to the one in other European countries, or the US?

BE: Historically, I think the photography market in the UK has been something of a younger sister to those in the United States, France, and even Germany to an extent. There are several reasons for this, not least the comparatively limited institutional visibility photography enjoyed in Britain for much of the twentieth century. Unlike in the United States, where institutions such as MoMA played a pivotal role in establishing photography within the museum from an early stage, the UK was slower to develop a comparable collecting and exhibition culture.

The commercial landscape has reflected this. We have had relatively few galleries dedicated exclusively to photography, and until more recently, even fewer contemporary art galleries incorporating it meaningfully into their programmes. This inevitably affects the development of a collecting culture and the confidence of the market.

That said, Britain has an extraordinary photographic heritage and is home to some exceptional contemporary practitioners. What I particularly value is the generosity of the photographic community here, especially the remarkable network of women photographers, curators, writers and educators who support one another. There is a genuine sense of camaraderie that I haven’t always encountered elsewhere.

However, I do think the commercial market continues to suffer from a lack of visibility, particularly within London’s gallery landscape and art fairs. Photography deserves a far more prominent place within the broader contemporary art market, rather than being treated as a separate or secondary discipline. This is something I feel quite strongly about, and I hope we will see meaningful change in the coming years.

As part of your job, you are working with all kinds of art-related people – collectors, artists, museum directors, art fair visitors etc.? Have you developed a certain routine to prepare yourself before entering a particular encounter/presentation/event?

BE: It rather depends on the occasion, but a good night’s sleep is always a useful starting point! I like to allow myself some quiet time beforehand to reflect, revisit my notes and think about the people I’m going to meet. If I’m moderating a conversation, I prefer to be thoroughly prepared but not overly scripted. The most interesting exchanges often happen when you allow a conversation to take an unexpected direction.
And, of course, a well-earned martini at the end of a long day, particularly after a successful talk or an intense day at an art fair, is something of a ritual!
What would you currently advise a collector of photography, now that photography auctions were moved to “online auction” only and the prices going down?

BE: My advice has always been to see as much photography as possible in person, with your own eyes. A photograph is, after all, a physical object, and no digital reproduction can adequately convey its scale, surface, tonality or material presence. Screens can distort colour and flatten subtle differences in printing techniques, all of which are fundamental to understanding and appreciating a work.

When considering vintage photographs, I would always encourage collectors to examine the work unframed wherever possible, including the verso. Stamps, signatures, annotations and other physical evidence can reveal a great deal about a photograph’s provenance, dating and authenticity. Equally, understanding the distinction between a vintage print and one made later, or between different printing processes, can have a considerable impact on value.

I would also encourage collectors to develop relationships with a small number of trusted photography specialists. The medium has its own particular complexities, and expert advice on condition, rarity, provenance and market history can be invaluable.

As for the market, I would be cautious about interpreting the shift towards online auctions, or softer prices in certain sectors, as evidence of a broader decline in photography’s importance. The market is nuanced, and exceptional works with strong provenance and historical significance continue to command attention. For collectors, periods of adjustment can also present opportunities. Ultimately, I believe in buying with curiosity, conviction and a genuine love of the work, rather than simply following market trends.
If you could freely pick a location – anywhere in the world – and curate a show without any limitation to the budget, which country and which location/museum would this be?
BE: Oh, what a wonderful question, and a difficult one! I think I would choose the Metropolitan Museum of Art or MoMA in New York, or perhaps, if we’re really dreaming, both simultaneously!

I would love to curate an ambitious exhibition exploring the history of photography in dialogue with painting, sculpture, drawing and design, demonstrating just how integral photography has been to the evolution of artistic practice across disciplines. Rather than presenting photography as a parallel history, I would want to show how deeply interconnected these histories have always been, and how photography has both absorbed and transformed the visual languages of other art forms.

One of the things I find most fascinating about the medium is its inherently experimental nature. Photography has continually challenged our understanding of representation, authorship and reality, and artists have often pushed it forward by returning to techniques developed at its very inception. There is something wonderfully paradoxical about that: the future of photography is frequently informed by its past.
I would want the exhibition to celebrate photography not simply as an art form in its own right, which of course it is, but as one of the great catalysts for change in the history of visual culture.
Photographer on your current watch list?

BE: I’m a huge admirer of Thomas Struth and remain fascinated by the way his practice continues to evolve. His ability to move between portraiture, architecture and the complexities of contemporary society, while maintaining such a distinctive visual language, is extraordinary.

Another artist I return to constantly is Helena Almeida. Although she sadly passed away in 2018, she left an extensive and intellectually rich body of work that continues to reveal new layers to me. Her exploration of the relationship between photography, painting, performance and the body feels as relevant today as ever.

Among younger artists, I’m particularly interested in Sara Sahores, Aisha Seriki, Isabelle Young and Yumna Al-Arashi. Each has a distinctive approach to image-making, and I enjoy following how their practices are developing.
Describe yourself with 1 word.
BE: Curious.
For more information, please follow Brandei on Instagram: @brandei_estes
About Brandei Estes Acting Senior Curator of Photographs, National Portrait Gallery, Independent Photographs Curator and Advisor.

With over twenty years of experience in the art world, Brandei Estes joined the National Portrait Gallery in early 2026 as Acting Senior Curator of Photographs (a post she will hold until December 2026). Previously she was the Head of Photographs at Sotheby’s (Europe, Middle East and Asia) for a decade, following an extensive career of working in photography and contemporary art galleries in London and Paris including Michael Hoppen Gallery, Brancolini Grimaldi and Nelson Freeman. Estes was instrumental at Sotheby’s in the growth of the Photographs sales in Europe and further afield, and was the lead business getter for the department. Her comprehensive role at Sotheby’s also included professional writing, research and all aspects of auction estimates, fair market value, charitable donation, and insurance appraisals.

Since 2024 Estes has worked independently curating photography exhibitions including the 2026 exhibition ‘Replaced’ by Diana Markosian at Gallerie d’Italia in Turin, Italy, as well as advising clients on how to build their photography collections. Estes also lectures throughout the year on collecting photographs and the photography market for public and private institutions, museums, galleries and fairs in the UK, Europe and USA. Estes is a nominator and judge for numerous international photography awards including the Prix Pictet, Deutsche Börse Photography Prize, the Deloitte Photo Grant and the Louis Roederer Photography Prize for Sustainability, and served for five years as the Chair of The Photographers’ Gallery Associate Patrons committee. In addition to sitting on the Curatorial Board of The Phair in Turin, Estes has been a member of Photo London’s Curatorial Board since 2023 and is a trustee of the Carol and Michael Storey Foundation, an ambassador for the Collezione Ettore Molinario in Milan, and sits on the art advisory board of Koko, London.
